utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Just one brief matter I would like to raise in relation to a disclosure issue. As Your Honour is aware, the Defence -- the witness has testified that the missing person reports have been provided to the Tribunal. The Prosecution tendered yesterday about 231 of those missing person reports related to the annex in the indictment. It came to the Prosecution's attention that 15 missing person reports were on the Prosecution system but didn't appear on the 65 ter list and, subsequently, the e-court system. Those 15 documents for the particular individuals were provided to the Defence yesterday or last night. And in relation to those 15 documents, 14 of those missing persons were identified at Ovcara, and one of those individuals was not identified at Ovcara. And that material has been given to the Defence. The Prosecution doesn't seek to tender those documents, nor does it view them exculpatory in any way. However, out of an abundance of caution, those documents, once discovered, were provided to the Defence last night and which, in fact, in relation to missing person reports, leaves another 16 that are outstanding in that sense. And that was discussed with the witness yesterday, and he said that approximately that number - I think it's approximately 20 - would be provided by the office, their office, as soon as possible, because the Prosecution hadn't received them. I just thought I would raise that matter. I've spoken with counsel last night about it, and advised them of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Before we get back to the main evidence today, could the Chamber mention that there is a need to adjust the timetable next week. It's all to do with me, I'm afraid, and other commitments that I have. Monday, as you know, is a holiday. We sit on Tuesday and Wednesday at the time we would normally sit on Monday; that is, from 12.30 to 5.00. That's Tuesday and Wednesday of next week. And on Thursday and Friday we sit from 9.00 to 1.45. Which is not, as it were, the advertised programme. Monday the following week we would revert to the normal timetable of 12.30 to 5.00, et cetera. Now, Mr. Grujic, may I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to inform you that in order to be as efficient as possible in our cross-examination, the Defence teams have split among themselves the topics for cross-examination in order to avoid any overlap, and we will see whether we manage to do that once we reach the conclusion of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, it seems to me that yesterday we had a good pace of questions and answers, given that what we say is interpreted, so we should probably stick to the same pace today.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, in view of the position you held in 1991 as described by you yesterday, I assume that you know that in September and December of 1991 Serbian civilians were killed in Sarvas and Paulin Dvor in the vicinity of Osijek. I assume that you know that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I of course am aware of that, but not through my position. Rather, through the job that I do, because my job involves the missing persons and there are some documents confirming what you say in the office that I am in charge of now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please let me know whether you and your commission took part in the exhumation of their mortal remains, and was any identification conducted?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the request of the International Criminal Court I conducted, or rather, organised an exhumation which was carried out based on the order of the relevant investigative judge in the location where the remains of the victims from Paulin Dvor was located. So everybody from that incident was identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The location where they were found is approximately 500 kilometres away from the place where they were killed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and that was clearly stated in the documents related to investigation. It was established that this was a secondary grave, which means that the remains were brought there from other location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please, in relation to this, please tell me, were these facts entered in one of your lists of the persons who perished during the aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the names of these people right now, but as the identification process unfolds, as the administration processes this, the names of these people are placed on the list of those who were killed. However, this grave is not on the list of graves that we presented here, the list containing 142 graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understood, thank you. What about the number of these people? Is the number included in the number of killed persons in Osijek and Baranja county?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, all of those who were identified, if the information reached us, just as they are placed in the list of 12.000 persons, they were also placed in other lists. The list for the Danube region, and then Vukovar, and then down to closer identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. You told us yesterday that you divided the Danube region into these two counties, so it's entirely clear to us. Do you know that in the fall of 1991 in Gospic there was also an incident where a large number of Serbian civilians were killed by the ZNG? Did you conduct any work pertaining to exhumation and identification of these persons?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not participate in that. As far as I know, a portion of work was conducted by the JNA colonel, Dr. Stankovic. He also conducted some exhumations with his team in Eastern Slavonia in 1991. Some mortal remains were removed from that location. Some were buried. As far as I know, the competent investigative magistrate conducted some steps in order to attempt to identify some of the victims. And this is part of the trial conducted in the Republic of Croatia, a trial for war crimes committed, and I think that the perpetrators were brought to justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. Yes, I'm aware of the fact that the perpetrators were tried, especially given that after that crime even the European Commission stepped in and challenged the recognition of Croatian independence. However, after Vukovar events in early 1992, Croatia was nevertheless recognized as an independent state. I'm interested in this now: The list of these Serbian civilian victims, was it included in the total number of victims in the course of the aggression against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was included to the extent that we were able to establish the identity of victims and if there is a death certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, let me reiterate that this is provisional list of the persons who were killed. This kind of list was used, and it was compiled based on the information available so far. Let me also mention that all of the cases you mentioned so far, even if these victims were not included on the list, that would have had no effect on the final number. Let me reiterate that all of the documents that reached us meant that we included these people on the list regardless of their ethnic background, religious background, or the events that led to their death.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I asked you about were just some of the cases, some individual cases, and perhaps they would not have affected the ratio in the analysis, but I'm interested in this: Were they all included in your lists? I took it that your answer that all of those who were identified were included in the lists of those killed during the aggression against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who were identified and whose documents reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your CV, which is part of your report, it says that at some point in 1992 you moved from the civilian security service to the SIS, which is the military security service. I would like to know something about the reasons for doing that. Are they related to your later appointment as president of commission for the missing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The single reason was that the decision of the then minister of police and defence stated that some of the personnel should move from the Ministry of the Interior to the Ministry of Defence. Based on that decision and that agreement that was reached, I was transferred with my job. I kept the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony yesterday you told us how these two commissions were formed in 1991, and then your commission put together all of their work in 1993. What I would like to know is if the work of the commissions from 1991 also included work to find missing persons as members of the parties to the conflict, or were these searches only limited to those from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course information had to be gathered on the missing and captured of the other side, because that was the basic mechanism in order to conduct talks and to resolve these issues, if you wish to resolve. Unfortunately, at that time that is how things proceeded, that prisoners were exchanged according to the principle of parity. So if you did not have two prisoners, you could not get two prisoners of your own in return. Unfortunately, that was the principle at the time as well as the one that applied to all other information. So of course you had to gather as much information as you could. Of course, this later changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Grujic. Yesterday you told us that the three main tasks of these commissions and then your commission of which you were the chairman or president in 1993, were actually the exchange of prisoners, the monitoring of the treatment and accommodation of prisoners of war, and also gathering and processing of information on missing persons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify. There were two commissions at the time. One was entrusted with repatriation and exchange of prisoners as well as the monitoring of the treatment of prisoners of war and the conditions of their detention. That was one commission. The other commission gathered and processed information on civilian and other victims and missing persons from the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then from 1993 the commission that you presided over dealt with all of these matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What I would like to know is if you're familiar with the findings of the commissions relating to the detention of members of the Serbian ethnic group by the ZNG and Croatian paramilitary formations. Do you know the localities and the figures for 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the information for 1991, but I could know the data for the whole period. As I said, what I know up to 1993 is based on what I could see from the documents. But I don't know whether I actually had access to the complete documentation on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And these documents, do they describe the conditions of the detention of these persons at the institutions where they were detained?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have such reports. But all of this can be seen from the report of the International Commission of the Red Cross, who was actually entrusted with visiting these places, seeing what the conditions were, and then after that they made certain suggestions and remarks to the authorities that were in charge of these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday in one of your answers you said that the first case of detention of a person was registered on the 23rd of January, 1991, and that the first person that was killed was recorded on the 31st of March, 1991, and the first missing person was recorded on the 10th of April, 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about what is there in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You then responded to a question by my learned friend that the violence from June 1991 intensified, that it escalated in September, and culminated in December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that these victims that were covered in this time period that we mentioned are part of these lists of yours of missing persons, detainees, killed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I said that the records -- I actually said what these records were and when they begin, meaning that the victims are those who could be established, and all of them are included in these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since you set the starting date when you received the first reports about certain events, and in view of this assessment of the intensity of the conflict that you expressed, can you tell us by month, starting from February, 1991, following this first case of detention, what the number of detainees was for February, March, April, June, 1991, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't really tell you that. I could if we made such analysis - this is not in dispute - but it was impossible to prepare that type of information in a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell us what the figures were for those killed month by month, or is it the same thing that applies to the detainees, that you cannot do that so quickly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at the figures and the mass graves that were exhumed, then you will easily be able to see what the figures were for each particular period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How can we see what the period is of the exhumed mass graves when we don't see when the persons were buried there, all we see is that they are found?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the Vukovar new cemetery, Novo Groblje, where 800 persons are buried, they are all buried and processed by members of the JNA until February, 1992. At the same time, there were -- there was information according to the place of disappearance, circumstance of disappearance, and also time of disappearance. So in the same way, we have compiled data on the graves that were found. So if we analyse the victims, what that would indicate is that they were actually killed in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I can agree with you that if we have information, we can analyse it and then probably we can draw different conclusions on that basis. It depends on the parameters used to analyse the information. But in these analyses that we're dealing with here now, they were not done in that way and from what I understand you are not able to provide this information to us now, and these would be the figures according to the months of 1991, and you cannot provide these figures for the entire region of Croatia or for certain regions such as Podunavlje region or you cannot provide these figures for the town of Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in the way that you are asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I put this question, Mr. Grujic, because I wanted to check and also look at the indicators which led you to conclude that the violence intensified in June, escalated in September, and culminated in December, which is what you said yesterday. This is what I'm asking you. From what I could see, you are not able to provide precise information on which your conclusion is based. Your conclusion is based on some sort of prior knowledge that you have.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my conclusion is based on my experience which stems from my duties, and is on the basis of information that I analysed and presented - analyses which were provided to you - and also on the basis of generally known facts, generally known, not only to me, but also to the public. It is known when the intense attacks on Vukovar began. It is known that they were intense from September onwards and until December. If we look at the time that the mass grave of Ovcara was created, that already indicates the intensity of the events. We're talking about 200 victims there. If we are not looking just at my experience, but at the facts which you have been provided with, 200 persons at Ovcara, 1991, November. 938 dead people found at the Vukovar cemetery, and buried, dating from the -- from December until February. At the same time, the Lovas farm, 24 persons from the same population -- from the same population where the new cemetery also is. I could even provide you with names, if that's what you're asking me, because these names were also presented to you. I'm talking about 14 graves, if I'm not mistaken, that we're discussing here. This is proof that this was precisely the way it was presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The conclusion that that is precisely the way it was presented is something that I cannot dispute in advance. All I'm saying is that we don't have analysis that would lead us to this conclusion because we don't have the information. But you talked about the new cemetery in Vukovar. Do you have information when these persons lost their lives, the persons who were buried in the Vukovar new cemetery, when did they lose their lives?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is a series of documents. I have already said that, as far as the new cemetery of Vukovar is concerned, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, their official institutions, sent us 1.000 odd files about the dead people in Vukovar, and these files contain the locations for some of them, the locations where they were found, which means that they were brought -- I mean, we can even say 28 killed from the mass graves in Gelesova Dol. This is the period of November. The mass grave at Trpinjska Ceska, 11 victims where prisoners of war were killed that were captured on the 18th of November. The mass grave at Velepromet, 19 victims. You have all the first and last names in the attachment, as well as the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I did not have the intention to deal with this segment. My colleague is going to deal with the killed persons. But we need to know here when these persons were actually killed, not when they were transferred from one grave to the -- to the other. So this would be the answer to the question on the escalation of violence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can establish that too. It's very clearly evident from the documents. The persons mentioned there, their files were sent to the court, and you have the dates that they were last seen alive in those records. If you would allow me, we cannot know the exact date when they were killed but we can make that estimate within a month or two of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I am going to allow my colleague to deal with this particular topic. All I was asking for were indicators for all groups, not only for those killed, but also for the missing and the detained, which led you to conclude about the escalation of such cases in the course of 1991. I embarked on this topic for a different reason, however. Because I see that the information that we are discussing about the detainees and the missing persons, which date from before the aggression on Croatia - and this is the 5th of August, 1991 - you included also that information in your data.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that these people were captured and registered as such. It's another thing that the law on defenders will not recognise their status and material rights for the period that the law is in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But we can agree that even before this date they were included in your lists and in the events before the 5th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is a normal thing, because the fact that they were captured is something that was established; it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then we cannot accept your assertion made to my learned friend that the information about the detainees and the missing had to do with the consequences of the aggression on the Republic of Croatia, because evidently according to the law of the Republic of Croatia on the defenders began on the 5th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot go into what the law provides for in terms of the period. What I'm talking about is the fact that a person who was connected to the armed conflict was placed in detention or in prison. This had to do with armed conflict. Not any other type of event, but armed conflict. And if you allow me, nobody says that we cannot find anyone that is still alive and that is perhaps still captured who was involved in the armed conflict, is anyone able to definitely rule such a thing out. And this will happen after the date provided for by the law, but it does not rule out the fact that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But the law recognises the status of the defenders from the beginning of the aggression on the Republic of Croatia, so the law is a kind of parameter delineating; the beginning of the aggression and which activities were connected with this aggression. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: The law was drafted in order to implement one's benefits. It does not prove anything as far as historical facts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My opinion, in view of these regulations on the date of aggression against the Republic of Croatia, then indicates that we could not count on -- count those detained before the 5th of August, 1991, and those which were captured after. Would you be able to agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. Given the rules of the international law on the same subject, on tracing and finding the missing persons, these rules provide that the reports on missing persons are accepted regardless of how some legal regulations limit the time duration of the conflict. The same rule applies in the International Committee of the Red Cross. Any other solution would, in fact, be in conflict with the norms of the international community and international organisations dealing with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: However, the question here is when did the aggression against the Republic of Croatia start. I don't think that there is any doubt that it started in August of 1991. That's what it says in the law. This is what the law defines. Armed conflicts began in August, 1991, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you said yesterday, this is something that the historians could debate at length. I'm testifying here about the facts pertaining to the detained and missing persons, and the records kept regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The data on the detained persons in the Republic of Croatia and in the Podunavlje region from August 1991 to the 30th of June, 1996, do you have this data?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have this data, but I have data on all persons which are recorded in this documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, your data covers the period from January, 1991, to the 30th of June, 1996.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, I will repeat: The first registered person in our records of the killed persons was recorded on the 31st of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm speaking of the detained persons.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in order to answer your question, I must say this as well, otherwise we are conflicting entirely what we have discussed so far. The person was killed violently on the 31st of March, 1991. If this was not an armed conflict, I don't know what it was. In February, 1991, we recorded the first displaced person. As for the missing persons, the first recorded case was on the 10th of April, 1991. And if you are interested in the location, it was in Glina, where at the time there were already such conflicts in place. As for the first detained person, the first detained person was recorded on the 23rd of January, 1991, and it was in prison until the 4th of August, 1995 -- no. I apologise; no, no. It was the 23rd of January, 1991, and this person was exchanged in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In April of 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the identity of that person?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I must have made a mistake. Now, speaking of detained person, out of 7.666 persons, the first recorded person was recorded on the 23rd of January, 1991. The last recorded person was on the 4th of August, 1995. The last exchange of prisoners took place in April of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in something you mentioned in your previous answer. Namely, you said that the first person was killed on the 31st March, 1991, and you believe that that was in the circumstances of armed conflict. Yesterday I put some questions to you about the attacks, explosions which took place in the territory of Osijek, and you said that that was within the competence of the Ministry of the Interior, it had to do with public law and order. I assume that a case of death can be caused by a plain murder, a plain crime of murder. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in this case we had an armed group belonging to an armed formation, and they attacked regular police force, and under the circumstances, this can only be called an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the area that we can discuss here. I suppose that you cannot give me a figure of total number of the detained from September of 1991 to late November, 1991, for the Podunavlje region or Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a month-by-month figure, but if you look at the facts concerning those detained in Vukovar, or rather, persons from Vukovar who were detained, then you will see that in the Mitrovica KP Dom, out of 1.656 prisoners, there were a certain number in Stajicevo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then just comparing these two figures, you will see that more than one-third of the detained were led away on the 18th of November. And from that date, for a period of 10 days, they were taken to various camps. They were taken to Begejci where there were 1.156 prisoners, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm now referring to the data given in your report and your tables. I don't see specific figures pertaining to this period of time, from September to November of 1991. I can't see, based on this, how many people were taken when to each of the collection centers, so I can't draw any conclusions about this. I suppose that you can't do that either right now, otherwise it would have been included in the tables that you presented here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of these things are possible. This can be done, but it just depends on which particular details you are interested in. My aim was to provide data for these four categories, to provide basic parameters which would clearly indicate the situation as it existed in general, as it existed in the Podunavlje region and in Vukovar, to give you some idea about the number of victims and their ethnic background. Also, we tried to categorise the victims to show whether they were defenders or civilians, to give you some idea about their gender. This is typical information provided for statistical purposes, and there are hundreds, maybe even thousands of angles that one could look at it from, depending on your needs. If you came to us with your specific needs, we would have provided the specific parameters that you are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Grujic. But I'm just trying to link this to the indictment in this case. This is why I'm referring to the period of time that we are interested in, based on the indictment, and that's why I asked you about this period of time. I fully agree with you that various parameters can be analysed, but we don't have this information here right now. Let us now please look at tab 2.1. This is Exhibit 539. It is related to the Podunavlje region. Could it be please put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, you said tab ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: 2.1, which is Exhibit 539. This is your report for the Podunavlje region. I am personally interested in this portion towards the bottom of the page which pertains to the detained persons. Let us now see whether everybody can see it on their screens. Very well. So towards the end of the page, towards the bottom of the page, we see the data on the detained, categorised by gender, age, and length of detention.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the conclusion that you reached in percentages is that 94 per cent of those detained were male and the rest were female, and that the majority of those detained, 89.42 per cent, were between 18 and 60 years old, and that in terms of the length of detention, up -- the people who were detained up to 30 days were 22.69 per cent; those detained up to a year, 70.08 per cent; and that only in 0.96 per cent of the cases people were detained longer than one year but not longer than two years. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the information that we compiled based on the general statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on these statistical figures, can we agree that it was mostly the men who were detained, those fit for military service, aged between 18 and 60, and that most of them were detained up to 30 days during which time it was decided whether there would be criminal proceedings instituted against them or not, and that if so, they were kept in detention for up to one year. And then the further outcomes were that they were tried and then either acquitted or the trial was never concluded.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about these trials that were conducted. That's one thing. The other thing that I can fully agree with you on has to do with the general population that was detained. However, we also must not ignore the fact that a large number of women left that area as refugees or displaced persons. Now, as for the length of detention, yes, this information here is accurate, but you also have to bear in mind that a large number of detainees, numbering 600 and more, that was led away on the 18th of November and exchanged six -- seven months later, which is to say that there were in triage for that period of time; quite long. But this number also has an impact on the general statistical data. This is what we provided, and you can draw different conclusions based on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Grujic. Yesterday on page 52, line 21 to 25, you said in examination-in-chief that out of these detentions, 45 per cent were conducted by the JNA, 25 per cent by paramilitary formations, and 25 per cent was unknown, or unrecorded. Do you remember saying this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As for the people who were detained by the JNA members, you said to us yesterday that some of them were kept in temporary transit camps until they were transferred to some detention centres or penitentiary centres. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, when it comes to terminology, I cannot agree with you. There were detention locations in Vukovar, such as Velepromet. It's a well-known fact. The barracks as well, and the Komerc facility. These were locations where people were detained. They were transported from these locations towards other places of detention which I wouldn't call detention centres, such as those Stajicevo and Begejci. The one in Sremska Mitrovica was a proper detention institution because it was a regular prison. As for Stajicevo and Begejci, they are agricultural farms and they cannot be referred to as detention centres, not proper ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, you misunderstood me. When I said detention centres or detention institutions, I was referring to the map that you enclosed with your report, depicting locations of detention. Let me find the exhibit number. It's Exhibit 543. I was referring to Nis, Valjevo, Sremska Mitrovica, Padinska Skela, Novi Sad, and detention institutions there. In the beginning of my question I mentioned temporary or transit centres such as those in Stajicevo and Begejci from where the detainees were transferred to other locations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is tab 2.8. It is clearly stated here, places of detention, 2.796 persons from Vukovar. These are places, locations of imprisonment. You called them institutions. I allow that. But if you permit me, the answer here is that almost 3.000 people, practically 40 per cent of the -- those imprisoned in the period of November, 1991. So we have actually now come to the answer that I was not able to provide earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I don't see on this diagram or chart when these people were imprisoned. I just see the location and the number, but I don't see when each one of them was imprisoned. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, you cannot see that here, but it is a generally known fact that all of those from Vukovar or those who were on the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for the most part were taken away in that period and on that day. And we can see that in the questionnaires for the missing and the detained, which you do have access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you that we have that at our disposal, those questionnaires. But what I can agree with is that analysis can be done. What I'm noting is that we do not actually have it at the moment. But, Mr. Grujic, could you please tell me, this analysis of the detained persons for the Podunavlje region and the indicators relating to the gender, age and length of detention would be similar as the one for the Osijek-Baranja and the Vukovar-Srijem counties. And the percentage would be similar for the actual town of Vukovar itself, you can agree with me?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the statistics that were given are more or less identical. They can be -- they reflect each other also in the way that they were compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We are talking about Vukovar now, and the detentions -- and we're talking about something that has nothing to do with these tables and that is that do you know that before the fall of Vukovar on the 17th of November, 1991, one of the topics of a meeting of the Croatian government was to allow the commissioner of the municipality of Vukovar to negotiate with Goran Hadzic on the surrender of the Croatian forces in Vukovar. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know any particulars on this topic. I can perhaps know as much as any average citizen would know about that, but not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In line with the duties you were performing at that time, do you know that Goran Hadzic was actually an associate of the JNA counter-intelligence group that was active on the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Srem and that he had a code-name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. I did not work directly on this, so I really cannot. It's possible that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to deal any more with that, we're going to come back to our statistics. You told us that the information about the number of detainees were compiled on the basis of several sources; on the basis of reports of exchanges in 1991, which were compiled by the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Croatia, then on the basis of records of exchanges conducted by the commission of which you were president, with the mediation of the Red Cross on the basis of reports on registered detainees drafted by the Red Cross at the actual locations of detention, and on the basis of statements by detainees themselves when they were submitting requests in relation to securing some rights arising from that status. Is that correct? Were those the sources used?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us the numbers or the percentages of the numbers of these persons receiving such status only on the basis of their statements.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean only on the basis of their statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that summing up the information of the detainees was done with problems in 1991 and that you received documents on the exchanges that you did receive. Then you mentioned these other sources on the basis of which you formed your records, and this list of detainees, but you also told us that a number of persons, after being released from detention, reported by making a statement that they were actually detained in order to gain some benefits and then you said that you signed those statements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't understand each other. What I said was - I don't want to repeat it - the sources that you mention now, but I also said that a number of persons who were released from detention, that means through exchanges - how else could they have been released? - that a number of such persons also provided statements on the basis of which we could get more information about the -- their period of detention and also about other people who were possibly detained. This is what I talked about, and not that we entered them into the records on the basis of their statements. Even to this day there is still a possibility of an administrative procedure whereby a person can subsequently be entered into the list or the records of prisoners of war or detainees, but this can be done only for persons about whom documents exist that they were exchanged, documents by the institution that conducted the exchange, or documents of the international organisation mediating in the exchange. A statement by a person who was in detention is not sufficient to have that person entered into the records. If I was not clear, I'm sorry, but I believe that I have clarified this matter a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite clear to us now. Does that mean that each person from your list of detainees has documents that you have just indicated, such certificates?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean certificate of detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certificate of detention or that they were recorded or registered in the institution of their detention.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each person that is on our list of detainees is on that list on the basis of information on exchange or release by authorised institution; the previous commission or our commission. A number of those persons has such confirmation by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear to me. Does that mean that you have all the documents, all the lists of exchanged persons from 1991 until 1996 when you said that the last exchange was carried out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For each person?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each person that was in prison has a file that contains the place, the time of detention, the circumstances of detention, possibly information that they saw such and such a person also in detention, that the commander of the camp was such and such a person. So information that a person in such a situation was able to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That is clear to me. Mr. Grujic, does that mean that each of these files that you are speaking about, file of detained persons, would contain the proof of detention or proof that they were recorded by the Red Cross at the location of detention, or confirmation of the exchange of that person --

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would just like to finish. And that there is no file that is open or outstanding with a person that has been recorded as detained only on the basis of their own statement or statement of another witness?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no one in the records who was entered into the records just by providing a statement that they or someone else were detained. That was not a way to be entered into the records. I repeat: Persons were registered on the basis of lists of exchanges and on the basis of records of the previous commission that conducted the exchanges, and these would be lists or files. We're not talking about files or dossiers, but we're talking about cards, registers that were transferred into electronic form, giving the first and last name, date of detention. No one is in the record because they came and said, "I was detained, so could you please put me on the records." This was simply unacceptable, then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So let us conclude so that it is quite clear to me. Does that mean that each person on that list as a detainee has a certificate of detention, a certificate of exchange, or a certificate of detention or a certificate of them being registered by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't have certificates, this is not our method of work. Nobody issued certificates of exchange. Exchanges were conducted in the following way: After the authorised organs reached an agreement, lists for exchanges were made. These exchange lists -- and that was the only document because there were no other data available. After the exchange was carried out, all the persons that were exchanged on that list were entered as exchanged persons. Some of the information is what it was at the point of exchange. Then we continued to expand these -- these records. When we would have a person that would need a certificate of exchange, then their personal data would be expanded with other necessary information that was required. So the list of detainees was formed on the basis of exchange lists drafted at the location of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the card or the dossier or file of every person, on the basis of information on exchange, says the record of exchange on such and such a date and such a such and location?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not say that. It says exchange on such and such a date at such and such a location, or liberated in the following circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any requests for the recognition of status of a detained person when a person did not have any of those certificates, no records by the Red Cross, or confirmation that they were detained in a certain institution, or confirmation that they were exchanged? Did you have such cases?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did we have such cases, we have them to this very day. Since I said that the commissions began to work in 1991, late 1991, there were detentions prior to that. These people were exchanged at the local level, and it was possible that some of those people were not entered into the records. In order to be fair and just, we decided that persons can be entered on the lists later, persons who were detained, but in order to include them on the list those persons had to provide valid documents, such as the document of the authorised institution carrying out the exchange or a document of the International Committee of the Red Cross, registering that person in detention or the way they were freed. Because there were cases when people, for example, were in prison in Sremska Mitrovica, were registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross, but for various reasons were freed, released. They were released and they left the prison before any exchanges took place. Such a person obviously was not on the list precisely because the person was not exchanged. But it's a fact that the person was in prison. In order to prove that, the person would secure certificate of registration in prison from the ICRC and on the time spent in prison, and such a person would then subsequently be entered into the register. This is a small number of cases, and we still have such requests of all those; however, all those who cannot meet the criteria cannot be entered on these lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A person who cannot obtain the certificates that you just talked about cannot be entered on the list of detainees and you did not include such persons on the list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, although I think that that is clear, that the Vukovar-Srijem region that we talked about does not totally correspond to the territory of the municipality of Vukovar from 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Or the territory of the Osijek-Baranja county does not completely correspond with the then territory of the municipality of Osijek in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Also, Eastern Slavonia and its territory in 1991 does not now fit into any of the newly-created counties. Actually its territory covers the territory of two or more countries at present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All these tables that you presented to us yesterday were regionally deployed and analysed according to the current counties and the boundaries of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you were totalling the information, you clearly used this principle. So the numbers from the population census of March, 1991, that I see were used when talking about the total number of population according to the counties were actually totaled according to the new administrative division of counties of the Republic of Croatia and not the one that was valid in 1991. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify this a bit. You mentioned Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar municipality. Now that we're talking of Vukovar and the Vukovar analysis, let's start with that. Had we analysed the then Vukovar municipality, which at the time had 29 locations or settlements, then the numbers of victims would have been larger. Which means, had we analysed all of these 29 settlements comprising Vukovar municipality, then the number of missing would be 423, where in Vukovar it would be 353.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a minute please, Mr. Grujic. I understand what you're trying to say now, but what I'm trying to say is that the figures that we have here do not pertain to the territory as it was in 1991, which means that they don't reflect the situation as it was in 1991, regardless of whether it was -- whether the effect would be to have larger numbers or smaller numbers. Whatever the outcome, you did not analyse the situation as it was in 1991 when the events took place. I hope that we can agree on this.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures here and the number of residents relate to the occupied portion of the Republic of Croatia. That is to say, Vukovar-Srijem county had or has two thousand three hundred one thousand two hundred forty-one thousand [as interpreted] residents, whereas the occupied portion had 101.000 and something residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us see if we understand this. This is not the number of residents who lived in the Vukovar municipality in its boundaries back in 1991. That's all I'm asking you, regardless of whether the number you're giving me is greater or smaller.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking of Vukovar, the town of Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I Gave my data for the town of Vukovar. I'm reiterating: The municipality of Vukovar at the time in 1991 had 29 settlements in its territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Grujic, based on your data, can you tell me, please, how many residents lived in Eastern Slavonia back in 1991 and what was the ethnic composition of the residents percentage-wise?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you about the occupied portion because we analysed the occupied portion. The occupied portion of two counties where there were the victims that we analysed. People did not go missing in the portions which were not occupied. So we are now referring only to the territory that was occupied, and all the information we provided is for that portion of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now it seems that a number of questions arise from your answer. First of all, I am interested in the number of residents and ethnic composition of residents in Eastern Slavonia. Can you give us these figures? Also, can you give us the figures for the number of residents and their ethnic composition in the occupied portion of Eastern Slavonia, as you are calling it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you this, these figures. The occupied portion of the Podunavlje region comprising two counties, Vukovar-Srijem county and Osijek-Baranja county. So the occupied portion back in 1991 had 193.135 residents. If we look at the county in whole or if we add up these two counties, then - just a minute - then it would be about 600.000 residents, and I can give you the precise figure, if you want. That is to say, I guess that's what you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Grujic. That's not what I asked you. It seems that we failed to understand each other. You spoke about the Podunavlje region and the occupied portions of two counties. And as far as I am aware, that covers the region of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia, and Western Srem. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that these figures pertain to the entire region and I'm interested in the figures for Eastern Slavonia, not in those for Baranja and Western Srem. And I think that, based on the tables provided by you, you can't give me those figures now. That was my question: You can't give me those figures for Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, let's try and clarify these geographic terms. If we're talking of Eastern Slavonia now, then we have to talk of Slavonia, which includes Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia. That's a geographical concept. What I told you here were figures for counties which now administratively cover the area that we're dealing with. How can I now give you data for Slavonia, Slovenia, or Austria, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, I didn't ask you randomly for Eastern Slavonia. I asked you because it is in our indictment. That's why I asked you about it. I didn't put that question to you in order to confuse you. No; on the contrary. As for Vukovar municipality, back in 1991, did it have 84.000 residents? To be more precise, 84.189. And that includes Vukovar municipality with the neighbouring villages.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I said 84.189.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you have such information in any of your lists?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't provide that figure to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the number of residents in Vukovar in August of 1991, those residing in Vukovar, as well as their ethnic composition? Also, can you tell us to what extent did the ethnic composition change from early 1991 to August 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only speak of the official data, the number of residents provided by the state Bureau for Statistics. What you asked me just now is something that nobody knows, nobody can give you even any assessments and it is up to demographers to come up with that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Grujic. However, the census from 1991 that you referred to was made for these geographical regions, not for counties which were established later.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The census that I was referring to was produced by the state Bureau for Statistics, and it pertains to 1991 when this data was published. I can't give you a month-by-month overview to tell you whether there were any changes in the movement of residents and what kind of changes, all I can tell you is that, yes, there were some changes in Vukovar, and I can tell you that on the basis of the number of displaced persons from that town. So if we look at that number and if we look at different periods of time, then, yes, in that case we can talk about the number of people who left Vukovar and their ethnic composition. And yes, I can do my calculations right here, right now, if you're interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grujic, it seems we misunderstood each other once again. I told you this: The data in 1991 that you used in your report pertained to different administrative boundaries than those that you analysed in your report. Can we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm telling you is that the data I provided here for the town of Vukovar were compiled just for the town of Vukovar, not for the administrative unit, municipality of Vukovar, which had 29 settlements. When we speak of the town of Vukovar, we are referring only to the inner, urban area, based on the data provided by the state Bureau for Statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And they date from when, this data of the state Bureau for Statistics?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1991, it says up there at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Grujic, I think that it will be up to somebody else to analyse this, and everybody knows that administrative borders were different in 1991 than later on. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic. We must now have the first break. And we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Grujic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mira Tapuskovic, I will be putting questions to you. Yesterday you told us that in 1991 in Croatia, as the state administration evolved, certain administrative changes were made, including organisational changes of the body that you were the president of. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in that position in 1993, and another organisational structure existed prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First it was a commission, then an office, and then an administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The material that accompanied your report stated that this body -- I will be using the term "body" so as not to refer specifically to the time when it was either a commission or an office or an administration. So, the material that accompanied your report indicates that this body compiled information, processed information, it kept records on the exhumed and identified persons, mortal remains, detained and missing persons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of the tasks within the scope of responsibility of the office were listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, in view of Croatian legislation, what did the task of processing data entail?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly speaking, the analysis of data. The analysis of data on all of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The decree from 2001 stipulated that that body has to keep records on the basis of a number of parameters, and that certificates could be issued by that body. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And that regulation is still in force. This body issues certificates on detained and missing persons. This is done pursuant to the request of the family members. Also, similar certificates can be issued concerning detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it's a kind of an administrative document that has certain force in administrative proceedings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the analysis of data, as one of the tasks performed by the body whose president you are, does that also include the verification of collected data?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that's due to the fact that the certificates issued by you have a certain legal force. That is to say, your body certifies the facts recorded.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. These documents, these certificates can be used in any legal transaction and can also be used in order to confirm the status which in turn entails certain effects and benefits.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you touched upon the questionnaires which were tendered into evidence here yesterday. Analysing your yesterday's testimony, I concluded that that was the basic document, the starting point when it comes to a missing person, and that it could lead to some other categories which were under the jurisdiction of your body.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. So that was a basic document, and on the basis of that document we launched tracing steps when it comes to missing persons, and then I said that missing persons could be found either alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That means that this questionnaire which was filled in by the persons initiating tracing, were the basic source of information for you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the basic source of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that the old questionnaires which were used between 1991 and 1993 proved to be incomplete; they did not have sufficient information. As a result of that, you embarked on this project to create new questionnaires; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the decision on doing that was adopted in 1993 and these questionnaires were put in use as early as in 1994?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to the helm of that institution I realised - not only I, the entire commission realised, that the information provided in order to trace somebody was insufficient, and that it needed to be harmonised with the regulations of the ICRC and other international bodies, and it was then the decision was made to improve this questionnaire in order to improve the quality of the information needed in order to trace somebody.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that the UN forms were used, and the ICRC forms as well, in order to create this new questionnaire. Can you please tell us now whether in your archives you still have old questionnaires.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these are not questionnaires. Rather, these are various lists and statements of family members. So mildly speaking, this is a disorganised documentation. Simply speaking, we did not have sufficient information in order to do quality tracing.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But this documentation, was it created in such a way as to pertain to an individual person or was it collective?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each person had its own records.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then please tell me whether your archives still have this documentation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we use it in order to conduct verifications, to compare data, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether all questionnaires which were submitted in this case, those that pertained to Ovcara, were compared to those dating from the period up to 1993? I'm saying "questionnaires" even though you said that those were not questionnaires, rather different types of documents.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, these earlier documents, early version documents, were they submitted to The Hague Tribunal at their request?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because these are old records which gave birth to new records, which are of much better quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that data collection from 1993 on was an organised campaign in about 102 branch offices of the Croatian Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 102 branch offices, plus about 10 collection centres where refugees were. We informed all embassies and consular offices about this campaign. All of embassies and consular offices of Croatia, in order to inform everybody of this campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you train the persons who filled in questionnaires or assisted persons who were tracing their family members in order to fill these questionnaires?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The office which created this new questionnaire carried out a training for those filling it. This is normally done when it comes to all questionnaires.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When The Hague Tribunal sought -- can you tell us, when did The Hague Tribunal sought these questionnaires from you? When they did that, I assumed that these questionnaires were scanned or copied. Did scanners exist at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, scanners did not exist at the time. They were photocopied and provided in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Reviewing these 200 and something [Realtime transcript read in error "100 and something"] questionnaires, which we as the Defence received, we noticed that what was added uniformly -- I would like to intervene. In the transcript, it would be line 25 on page 38, I said "200 and something," and it says "100 and something." Thank you. Most often on page 2 there was a uniform entry of asterisks or the phrase "turn over." Can you please tell us, if you had the questionnaires in your hand, what this particular thing would indicate.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the instructions or advice to those doing the interviews was that if a person filling in the questionnaire wished to say something which was not included in the questions, they could then use the asterisks and then on the empty page could note down all the remarks, all the requests that the person filling in the questionnaire would make.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that all the additional pages were photocopied and given to The Hague Tribunal as well as can you confirm that additional remarks of the persons filling in the questionnaires were noted down on the back of the questionnaires while only the facing page was actually copied?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say anything about that. The copying was done by those who were doing the interviews. They were present during the photocopying, they did the photocopying themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that because the documents that we received do not contain these additional comments, so what I wanted to see is whether, if you know that the information that we received, these forms, are incomplete. In any case, can you please tell us what the response was to filling in the questionnaires in 1993 in terms of Vukovar, specifically Ovcara, compared with the first period when the questionnaires were being filled in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "the first period"?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you such an analysis at this moment, comparison between the first database and the second database on Ovcara. We have a new database now, and you know that out of 264 persons, 262 questionnaires were filled in. So we can't discuss the absolute existence of questionnaires in relation to the names mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the requests or interviews filled in in relation to Ovcara until 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that we cannot know. As I said, the information was sketchy, no locations or circumstances were noted, and precisely that was the reason why we sought the questionnaires to be filled in again in this way. Because it's practically impossible to find this information in the old questionnaires.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your report you said that the media also participated in the whole procedure; newspapers, television, and that there was also a TV spot produced on this.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember that when the spot was broadcast and when the messages were broadcast, so that you would get the largest number of people to respond and to fill in these questionnaires, whether documentary films were shown on television about the suffering on the territory of Croatia during the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The press published these notices or advertisements on special pages at the explicit request to do that. I cannot really talk about how this was treated in relation to daily events. They were probably covered too. As far as television is concerned, I know that we specifically requested the spots to be broadcast at peak times, at prime time, and prime time on television is usually when news shows are broadcast, so this TV spot was broadcast just before the evening news. I don't know whether it was also broadcast before some documentary films or other types of programmes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me with certainty that the propaganda activities of the Croatian media at that time did not significantly influence the contents of the information that was entered in the questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that with certainty. I personally organised this media campaign, and the only purpose of the campaign was to get the greatest number of people involved and to get them to respond so that we could obtain this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to turn to tab 1.6, and could we look at Exhibit 535 on the screen. That is the questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And before we see the questionnaire on the screen --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a question on the persons who were the commanders of forces taking away the sought person. That was the question. That should be on page 3, because page 1 is not marked. The number of the page is actually 2. I asked you about the influence of the media on the veracity and the entry of information that the questionnaires contain. And I did that because in one of the questionnaires - and Mr. Grujic, we will try to mention names as seldom as possible and we will try to do all of this through numbers, thank you - we're talking about person -- person 697, according to the 65 ter number, and the ERN number in English is 0100-6078. In response to a question, who was the commander who took away the person sought, it is said that it was Vance Owen. Mr. Grujic, you don't have that. I didn't ask for that document to be placed on the monitor, because that would take a lot of time. But I did provide the information for the Trial Chamber and for my learned friends from the Prosecution about exactly which form we're talking about so they will be able to find it easily. Since you have already told us that all the information was verified, would it be an alarming thing for you to learn that somebody wrote that the commander of the units that took away the sought person was Vance Owen? Of course we know this is Cyrus Vance and David Owen; these are two different people. The person who signed the questionnaire, would you warn them about the inaccuracy and the illogical nature of that particular piece of information?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I been the interviewee, I probably would have the -- said yes. But since you have put this question to me, allow me to just say a couple of things. This same questionnaire, could you please look at the education of the person who provided this information. This is one thing. I don't believe that that person would know who we're talking about. Even the name wasn't given properly. So when we had responses like this, and we did have responses like this, what we need to know is that the questionnaires were compiled exclusively for the purpose of seeking persons. They were not made for any kind of court proceedings where we are using them now. The question that you mentioned was placed into the questionnaire for only one reason, and that was that during negotiations it would be possible then to say to the other commission, gentlemen, we have information that for 50 or 100 persons the name of a certain person is mentioned who commanded the unit who could have been responsible for that, so could you please check that so you could provide an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that was the point and the purpose of that question?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you about the point and purpose of the question, and this is, at least for me, not in dispute here when we're talking about the level of education of a person that is looking for someone. What we're talking about is the level of training of the person who is filling in the interview, and who, in a way, would need to assist the person providing the information for the interview, and who is seeking a close relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to intervene for the record. This is page 43 line 14, and line 14 starts as question, line 15 starts as answer, and we have information that should be the other way around. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you now is to turn to page of the questionnaire where you can see question number 18. And that is the question, "What would be the eventual categories that the sought person belonged to?" Can you please tell us, did you find that, Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us now what is the category next to the letter f) "Domobran," Home Guard?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the categories or names in that question, except for members of the civilian protection and civilian, refer to official armed forces of the Republic of Croatia and to the Home Guard. That was a formation bearing that name at that time, and that's what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when this formation was formed and who formed it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say when it was formed, but as such it is included in the official armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, just like the ZNG, and we even have a category for "other defenders of the Republic of Croatia" as a category because at that time different names were given to units and we allowed the possibility for people to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any reasons for not mentioning another category, the HOS? Because all the questionnaires that we received we also have articles for Ovcara 92, 93, 96, 104 and 142 that the persons being -- being sought did refer to HOS, but for number 92, referring to Ovcara, we did receive confirmation for the Ministry of the Defence that this -- the HOS is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: IVAN GRUJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be under section g), that's the category under which you could entry HOS or the Frankopan unit or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
